topic: Handheld active tremor cancellation: Micron 3-DOF system design and bench characterisation
citation: MacLachlan RA, Becker BC, Cuevas Tabarés J, Podnar GW, Lobes LA Jr, Riviere CN. Micron: an actively stabilized handheld tool for microsurgery. IEEE Trans Robot. 2012;28(1):195-212.
task_or_setup: 3-DOF parallel piezo manipulator in a 40 g handpiece moves a ~40 mm tool tip relative to the handle; 2 kHz optical PSD tracker (ASAP) measures handle and tip pose in world frame; Internal Model Control position servo at 2 kHz in link-length space with charge-controlled piezo drive; frequency/step responses obtained by injecting simulated handle motion numerically into the running loop; servo tracking error measured against a pre-recorded tremor disturbance
participants_or_bench: Bench/system identification; no human subjects for these numbers
comparator: Two controller tunings (critically damped vs underdamped); theoretical 'delay-only' canceller with the same 3 ms delay
key_quantitative_findings: Actuators: six Thunder TH-10R laminated piezo bending actuators (2 in series per leg x 3 legs), -240 to +480 V, 4 mA peak; force >1 N; slew rate >100 mm/s; tip workspace extent ~2 mm but largest enclosed cube ~400 um per side; actuator travel +/-400 um; kinematic calibration error 40 um RMS. Sensing: 2 kS/s pose, 4 um resolution (abstract); LED noise 0.74 um RMS (1 kHz bandwidth); tip noise 5.7 um RMS (full bandwidth), 1.8 um RMS (100 Hz bandwidth); 4 cm tracking workspace. Loop: identified pure delay 2 ms; nominal delay 8 cycles = 4 ms incl. inverse filter; closed-loop servo bandwidth 84 Hz (critically damped, phase margin 64 deg) to 123 Hz (underdamped, PM 42 deg, 5 dB peaking); first lateral resonance ~150 Hz, ~400 Hz resonance depends on tip mass. Performance: hand-motion attenuation >=15 dB (fivefold); 3D servo tracking error vs pre-recorded tremor 4.8 um RMS / 41 um max (underdamped) and 6.1 um RMS / 62 um max (critically damped); induced tip noise 1.6 / 1.2 um RMS; 200 um handle step gives 70 um overshoot (underdamped). Authors: in the <30 Hz band the servo is a pure delay, so rejection can only improve by reducing delay or predicting the disturbance.
units_and_conditions: Tip position in world frame from the same optical tracker (induced noise measured with a fibre-optic displacement sensor); RMS and maximum as labelled; 'bandwidth' = closed-loop position-servo bandwidth, not tremor band; physiological tremor; tip in free space (no contact load); attenuation declines above ~4 Hz because of delay
locator: Author manuscript: Abstract p1; Sec II.B p5 and Fig. 10 (actuator, force, slew, workspace, 40 g); Sec II.D p6 (tracker noise); Sec II.H p8 (+/-400 um, 40 um RMS); Sec II.J p8 (2 ms delay); Sec II.K.3 p11 and Table III (4 ms, 100/200 Hz tunings); Sec II.N p11-12, Table IV, Figs 23-26 (84/123 Hz, PM, tracking error, noise, step)
limitations: Handle-motion responses synthesised numerically (no physical shaker); reference sensing is an external line-of-sight optical tracker; 50 mm housing diameter and high-voltage drive; poorly damped resonances cap bandwidth; authors state suppression is delay-limited
relevance_to_design: Reference architecture for world-referenced closed-loop tip stabilisation; quantifies what ~2-4 ms loop delay and ~100 Hz servo bandwidth buy (>=15 dB) and shows the residual is set by delay
transferability_reason: Servo/IMC and saturation-management principles transfer and the +/-0.2-0.4 mm travel is similar to our +/-0.5 mm; but the world reference is an external 2 kHz optical tracker a pen cannot carry, the tip never touches a surface (mN or zero load vs 0.2-2 N), and -240/+480 V drive and 50 mm housing are not pen-compatible
design_implication: Budget total sensing-to-nib delay at <=3-5 ms if >=10-15 dB rejection at 8-10 Hz is required; target >=80-100 Hz closed-loop nib bandwidth with first resonance >=150 Hz; copy Micron's saturation handling (filter cut-off raised from 50% travel, alternate-goal substitution)

lead_verification: re-verified by lead against author manuscript PDF 2026-09-27 (84-123 Hz bandwidth, +/-400 um travel, 15 dB)

topic: Handheld active tremor cancellation: Micron 3-DOF human-in-the-loop evaluation
citation: MacLachlan RA, Becker BC, Cuevas Tabarés J, Podnar GW, Lobes LA Jr, Riviere CN. Micron: an actively stabilized handheld tool for microsurgery. IEEE Trans Robot. 2012;28(1):195-212.
task_or_setup: Hold still 30 s; trace a 500 um circle for 60 s; move 600 um and hold 15 s (x4); tip kept just above a laser-engraved rubber target (no contact); 27 G needle (400 um shaft); 29x stereo microscope with oblique-light shadow cue; conditions: off, low-pass goal filter (1.5 Hz), 'scaling' shelving filter (fL 0.15 Hz, fH 2 Hz, gain 1/3), both with 1 mm/s goal-velocity limiter; nested Latin square; 6 sessions per subject, sessions 4-6 analysed; logged at 200 Hz; not blinded
participants_or_bench: 6 humans: 3 ophthalmic surgeons, 3 novices (healthy, physiological tremor)
key_quantitative_findings: Scaling vs off: 3D max error 291 -> 157 um (-46%), 2D max 219 -> 105 um (-52%), 3D RMS 85 -> 58 um (-32%). Low-pass vs off: 3D max 229 um (-21%), 2D max 164 um (-25%), 3D RMS 77 um (-10%). Move time 2.9 s (off) -> 3.5 s (low-pass, +18%) -> 4.0 s (scaling, +37%). Handle (hand) motion rose 87.1 -> 117.6 um with scaling (+35%, significant). Hold-still 3D max motion -44% at tip and -30% at the sclerotomy. Normal microsurgical tremor is 'several hundred microns peak-to-peak'; eye-hand loop critical frequency 0.5-2 Hz; low-pass corner below ~1 Hz felt 'bouncy' and near-unusable at 0.5 Hz; 90% of tip speeds <2 mm/s; 1 mm/s exceeded 30% of the time.
units_and_conditions: Error = tip position relative to target from optical tracker, pooled across tasks; 3D/2D maximum and 3D RMS as labelled; physiological tremor under 29x magnification; free space
locator: Author manuscript: Abstract; Sec I.A-B p1-2 and Figs 1-3 (tremor, eye-hand loop, speed CDF); Sec II.F p7 and Table II (filters); Sec III.A p13; Table VI p14 (error metrics); Table VII p15 (move time, hand motion); Sec III.B.2 p14 (sclerotomy); Sec IV p16
limitations: Healthy physiological tremor only; no tip contact; unblinded; earlier controller version; n=6; slow visually guided microsurgical motions
relevance_to_design: Net human-in-the-loop benefit (10-52% error reduction) is much smaller than bench handle-to-tip attenuation (>=15 dB) because users slow down and move the handle more when loop gain is reduced
transferability_reason: Human adaptation effects (slowing, larger handle motion) are likely to recur in writing; but goal filters were tuned for slow visually guided microsurgery (1.5 Hz corner, 1 mm/s limiter) and would erase handwriting strokes; no pathological tremor; no paper contact
design_implication: Judge the pen on humans writing, reporting writing speed and handle motion as well as trace error; do not copy Micron's low-pass/scaling goal filters; tremor-band (adaptive notch/predictive) cancellation that passes voluntary strokes is required

topic: Handheld active tremor cancellation: 6-DOF Micron with piezo ultrasonic linear motors and side-load tolerance
citation: Yang S, MacLachlan RA, Riviere CN. Manipulator design and operation of a six-degree-of-freedom handheld tremor-canceling microsurgical instrument. IEEE/ASME Trans Mechatron. 2015;20(2).
task_or_setup: Gough-Stewart platform driven by six SQUIGGLE SQL-RV-1.8 piezo ultrasonic lead-screw motors; PID in link-length space with fifth-order duty-cycle linearisation; clamped tests: +/-2 mm sinusoids at 1-5 mm/s; side loads 0-0.3 N applied at a remote centre of motion 30 mm above the tool mount while tracking +/-1 mm at 1 mm/s; handheld pointing task 20 s at 25x with a fixed goal (all motion rejected); automated circle tracing 1-4 mm diameter
participants_or_bench: Bench (clamped) + 1 subject without surgical training for handheld tasks (5 trials)
key_quantitative_findings: Motors 2.8x2.8x6 mm, stall >0.3 N at 3.3 V (+/-0.5 N assumed in simulation); motor stroke 5.3 mm; tip workspace cylinder 4 mm dia x 4 mm; manipulator 23 mm dia x 37 mm, 14.4 g (moving parts 2.3 g); instrument 28.5 mm dia x 126 mm, 70 g; design side load 0.2 N (scleral entry). Optical tracker 1 kHz, <10 um RMS noise, 27 cm3. RMS tracking error vs side load (1 mm/s): 6, 6, 10, 15, 17, 17, 47 um at 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30 N; 0.15 N tolerated over whole workspace. Clamped RMS error 6-11 um at 1 mm/s, 7-22 um at 2 mm/s, 9-43 um at 5 mm/s. Handheld pointing: RMS 112+/-8 -> 12+/-2 um (89.3%), max 361 -> 49 um. Automated circles 10-20 um RMS (>20 um at 4 mm, 5 mm/s) vs manual 105-140 um. Cancelling 'currently limited by a chattering instability in the range of 50-100 Hz'; closed-loop bandwidth and latency not stated.
units_and_conditions: Tip position error from optical tracker, RMS and max; lateral side load applied at the RCM on the shaft, not a normal load at the tip; free space; pointing used a fixed goal (no voluntary motion passed)
locator: Abstract; Table I (spec); Sec II-III (motor, stroke 5.3 mm, 0.2 N design load, Fig. 3); Sec IV (control, linearisation, Fig. 8); Sec V.A Table II (side load); Sec V.B Table III; Sec V.C and Fig. 10-11 (handheld); Sec VI (chattering 50-100 Hz)
limitations: Handheld data n=1; fixed-goal pointing overstates benefit for tasks with voluntary motion; stick-slip ultrasonic motors caused chattering; loads applied laterally at the RCM; external tracker
relevance_to_design: Only handheld tremor canceller with quantified lateral-load tolerance in the 0.1-0.3 N range, i.e. the low end of plausible nib friction loads
transferability_reason: mm-scale travel, 70 g mass and ~0.25 N load tolerance are pen-relevant, but error rose to 47 um at 0.30 N, stick-slip motors limited bandwidth (chattering 50-100 Hz), the load is not a frictional tip contact, and sensing is external
design_implication: Size nib actuators for >=2-3x the worst-case lateral friction at 2 N normal load and measure error-vs-lateral-load curves like Table II; treat stick-slip (inertial/ultrasonic) actuators as high-risk for 4-12 Hz cancellation

topic: Handheld active tremor cancellation: 6-DOF Micron handheld performance when voluntary motion must be preserved

task_or_setup: 6-DOF Micron; hold still 20 s above a rubber target; trace a 500 um circle for 20 s; eye-phantom hold with RCM constraint; goal filters: low-pass (1.5 Hz corner, high attenuation beyond 10 Hz) and motion scaling (unity gain <0.15 Hz, ~1/3 from 0.15-2 Hz) vs unaided; 5 trials per task/mode; surgical microscope
participants_or_bench: Number of participants not explicitly stated (text refers to 'a participant')
key_quantitative_findings: Hold still (rubber target): 3D RMS 93 um unaided -> 61 um low-pass -> 40 um scaling; max 301 -> 192 -> 103 um (scaling max = 34% of unaided, p=0.003). Circle tracing: unaided 86 um RMS / 244 um max; max error 70% (low-pass) and 51% (scaling, p=0.02) of unaided. Control bandwidth limited by chattering instability at 50-100 Hz.

topic: Micron in tissue contact: hybrid position/force control (tip loads handled by active handheld tools)
citation: Wells TS, Yang S, MacLachlan RA, Lobes LA Jr, Martel JN, Riviere CN. Hybrid position/force control of an active handheld micromanipulator for membrane peeling. Int J Med Robot Comput Assist Surg. 2016.
task_or_setup: Membrane peeling on PDMS phantom and chicken-egg inner shell membrane with 6-DOF Micron plus 2-DOF fibre-Bragg-grating force-sensing tool; position loop with 1.5 Hz low-pass goal; force PID at 1 kHz engaged above threshold; soft/hard force limits 2/4 mN (phantom) and 2/6 mN (egg); 16x microscope
participants_or_bench: 4 (1 retinal surgeon, 3 non-clinicians)
comparator: Micron position control (tremor cancellation) without force loop
key_quantitative_findings: FBG sensor 0.25 mN resolution, 2 kHz, 0.71 mm diameter. Phantom: RMS force -32% (x) / -41% (y), max force -46% / -63%; position-control max 7.5+/-2.7 mN (x), 10.0+/-3.5 mN (y). Egg membrane: RMS -34% / -36%, max -54% / -58%; max 15.7+/-5.5 -> 7.2+/-1.4 mN (x), 12.5+/-5.3 -> 5.2+/-1.3 mN (y). Duration unchanged (p=0.57, 0.72); tears 1.4+/-1.4 vs 0.8+/-1.1 (n.s.). No friction or stick-slip analysis.
units_and_conditions: Lateral tool-tip contact forces in mN on soft membranes
locator: Methods (sensor, controller gains, constraints); Results (force tables/figures)
limitations: Contact forces 2-16 mN on compliant tissue; no rigid-surface friction; small n
relevance_to_design: Highest-load contact use of an active handheld stabiliser located: still ~100x below nib loads
transferability_reason: Forces (<=16 mN) and soft tissue are one to three orders of magnitude below 0.2-2 N frictional nib contact on paper; no evidence on stability of a position servo against Coulomb friction
design_implication: Assume nothing about Micron-style servo stability in frictional contact; develop and test a friction-aware position/impedance controller with nib normal-load sensing from scratch

topic: Causal tremor estimation: Kalman-filter state estimation with velocity feedforward in Micron
citation: Becker BC, MacLachlan RA, Riviere CN. State estimation and feedforward tremor suppression for a handheld micromanipulator with a Kalman filter. Proc IEEE/RSJ Int Conf Intell Robots Syst (IROS). 2011:5160-5165.
task_or_setup: 3-DOF Micron hold-still at a fixed 3D set point; PID feedback vs feedback + feedforward of Kalman-estimated handle velocity (u = u_FB + alpha*u_FF); controllers switched at random every 5 s without informing the operator; ground truth = tip position through 100 Hz zero-lag 2nd-order Butterworth; chirp 1 Hz-1 kHz injected into pose for frequency response; clamped-in-vise baseline
participants_or_bench: 1 operator familiar with Micron, no surgical experience
comparator: PID feedback only; clamped (no tremor) floor
key_quantitative_findings: Model: linear KF, constant-acceleration model (position, velocity, acceleration) per translational axis and constant-angular-velocity per Euler angle = 15 states; separate KFs for tip and handle; actuator input rotated into world frame in the tip filter; run at 2 kHz on ASAP data (2 kHz, <10 um RMS). Delay compensation: no explicit multi-step predictor; feedforward of estimated handle velocity anticipates disturbance during actuation latency. RMS tip error 7.9 um (feedback) -> 3.4 um (feedback+feedforward) = -56.7%; clamped floor 1.4 um; about -7 dB additional attenuation at 10 Hz; error spectrum rises near 60 Hz (Bode integral); 10-20 um tremor disturbances reduced to 5-10 um.
units_and_conditions: 3D tip position error vs set point, RMS (um); physiological tremor; free space; Micron range quoted as 2x2x1 mm
locator: Sec II.C (ASAP); Sec III.A eqs (10)-(13) (KF); Sec III.B eqs (14)-(18) (feedforward); Sec IV.B-C; Table I; Figs 4-6
limitations: n=1; hold-still only (no voluntary motion); relies on world-frame optical tracking; hand-set covariances
relevance_to_design: Shows a lightweight model-based estimator can halve residual error when the servo is latency-limited
transferability_reason: A 15-state linear KF with velocity feedforward is sensor-agnostic and cheap enough for a pen MCU with IMU and nib-position sensing; the only non-transferable part is the external world reference
design_implication: Build disturbance-velocity feedforward from a state estimator into the nib controller from the start and A/B it against pure feedback on the pen bench using identical tremor playback

topic: Inertial-only handheld canceller: first Micron prototype (IMU + open-loop piezo stacks + WFLC)
citation: Riviere CN, Ang WT, Khosla PK. Toward active tremor canceling in handheld microsurgical instruments. IEEE Trans Robot Autom. 2003;19(5):793-800.
task_or_setup: Pen-sized instrument with all-accelerometer 6-DOF inertial sensing, WFLC-based estimation at 1 kHz, open-loop 3-DOF parallel piezo-stack manipulator; mounted on a cam-driven oscillating plate (~9 Hz); tip tracked with ASAP
participants_or_bench: Bench, 12 trials per test
key_quantitative_findings: Prototype 170 g, 210 mm long, 22 mm mean diameter (second prototype 130 mm, 19 mm, 100 g). Actuators: TS18-H5-202 stacks (5x5x18 mm, ~14.5 um at 100 V, 50 us response, up to 840 N), 7 per actuator -> >=100 um per axis; manipulator trajectory tracking 2.5 um (1-D) and 11.2 um (3-D) RMS. topic: Causal tremor estimation: WFLC/FLC adaptive canceller (bench cantilever)
citation: Riviere CN, Rader RS, Thakor NV. Adaptive canceling of physiological tremor for improved precision in microsurgery. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng. 1998;45(7):839-846.
task_or_setup: 1-D stainless cantilever (28 mm) whose base is moved by a voice coil replaying recorded surgeon hand motion; two piezo elements (12.7x18.3x0.19 mm) at the base cancel; Hall-effect sensor at the tip; WFLC with 6th-order elliptic 7-13 Hz band-pass pre-filter estimates tremor frequency; FLC without pre-filter generates the cancelling command; 1 kHz sampling; 15 s tests
participants_or_bench: Bench; 25 unfiltered hand-motion recordings from 5 experienced eye surgeons (simulated vitreoretinal surgery) plus synthetic signals
comparator: Uncompensated beam; offline zero-phase 2.25 Hz low-pass 'voluntary' estimate
key_quantitative_findings: 10 Hz sinusoid (~12 um p-p): -71.8% RMS; 8.5-11.5 Hz modulated sine: -63.1%; high-passed tremor: -40.6+/-8.6%; 25 raw recordings: 6-16 Hz band RMS 2.2 -> 0.8 um (-66.9+/-15.6%, p<0.01) and RMSE vs voluntary estimate 5.1 -> 3.4 um (-30.4+/-14.0%). Phase: cancelling FLC path is 'zero-phase'; pre-filter lag affects only the frequency estimate (stated negligible). Hall sensor noise ~2 um p-p; beam resonance ~312 Hz excited; loading by tissue contact 'not dealt with'.
units_and_conditions: Beam-tip displacement (Hall sensor), RMS in um; physiological tremor of a few um; 1 kHz; free space
locator: Abstract; Sec II.A (WFLC, pre-filter); Sec II.B-C (bench, 1 kHz); Sec III, Tables I-II; Sec IV (sensor noise, 312 Hz, contact caveat)
limitations: 1-D bench; um-scale physiological tremor; ideal tip sensing; single-dominant-frequency model; no contact
relevance_to_design: Foundational MCU-cheap causal quasi-periodic canceller with near-zero in-band phase
transferability_reason: Algorithm ports directly to a pen MCU, but amplitudes, single-frequency assumption and free-space bench differ from multi-frequency non-stationary ET/PD tremor during writing (see ACT-09, ACT-14)
design_implication: Implement WFLC/FLC as the causal baseline, test with recorded pathological writing tremor at up to +/-0.5 mm, and report tremor-band and whole-trajectory error separately as done here

topic: Causal tremor estimation: BMFLC vs WFLC (+RLS/Kalman variants) and voluntary-motion separation delay
citation: Veluvolu KC, Ang WT. Estimation of physiological tremor from accelerometers for real-time applications. Sensors. 2011;11(3):3020-3036.
task_or_setup: Offline one-step-ahead (k+1) estimation on recorded tremor with WFLC, WFLC-Kalman, BMFLC-LMS, BMFLC-RLS, BMFLC-Kalman (band 7-14 Hz, frequency spacing 0.1); pointing and tracing tasks recorded with optical M2S2 (0.7 um resolution, 250 Hz), wrist rested; test data zero-phase band-pass filtered 6-14 Hz before estimation 'for sake of ideal comparison'; separate voluntary/tremor separation on raw data
participants_or_bench: 6 microsurgeons + 6 novice subjects, 2 trials per task
comparator: WFLC, WFLC-Kalman, BMFLC-LMS; causal and zero-phase 2 Hz low-pass for voluntary separation
key_quantitative_findings: Estimation accuracy (surgeon #1 example): WFLC 90%, WFLC-Kalman 93%, BMFLC 94%, BMFLC-RLS 99%, BMFLC-Kalman 99.5%. Mean RMS error, surgeons: WFLC 0.956+/-0.441, WFLC-KF 0.632+/-0.263, BMFLC 0.408+/-0.201, BMFLC-RLS 0.076+/-0.051, BMFLC-KF 0.003+/-0.002 um (novices similar). Voluntary separation on raw data: BMFLC delay 0.082 s (RMSE 4.61 um) vs causal 2 Hz low-pass 0.2 s (17.8 um); surgeon example 0.072 s (6.63 um) vs 0.186 s (26.5 um). Authors: real-time band-pass pre-filtering 'causes delay and it decreases the accuracy'; tremor showed multiple dominant frequencies in 7-11 Hz (2-5 Hz wide).
units_and_conditions: Tip displacement (um) from optical sensor; one-step prediction at 250 Hz (4 ms); physiological tremor; offline
locator: Sec 2 (data, M2S2); Sec 4 (Figs 5-6 delays; parameters; Fig. 7 accuracies); Table 1 (RMSE)
limitations: Non-causal zero-phase pre-filtering of test data and a 4 ms horizon make accuracies optimistic; physiological, not pathological, tremor; offline
relevance_to_design: Shows multi-frequency Fourier banks beat single-frequency WFLC and quantifies the tens-of-ms cost of causal voluntary/tremor separation
transferability_reason: BMFLC-Kalman is MCU-friendly and suits IMU data in a pen, but headline accuracies come from idealised non-causal pre-filtering and would not survive a causal pipeline with real pen latency
design_implication: Adopt BMFLC-Kalman as a baseline but evaluate all estimators on raw, causally processed pen data at the measured loop delay; budget tens of ms for any explicit voluntary/tremor separation unless a predictor covers it

topic: Learned tremor estimation: PHTNet deep bidirectional GRU (pathological tremor)
citation: Shahtalebi S, Atashzar SF, Samotus O, Patel RV, Jog MS, Mohammadi A. PHTNet: characterization and deep mining of involuntary pathological hand tremor using recurrent neural network models. Sci Rep. 2020;10:2195.
task_or_setup: 4-layer bidirectional GRU (400 hidden features), 4 s input windows at 100 Hz, trained to output the voluntary component one sample ahead; training/test targets built by adding synthesised voluntary sinusoids (amplitude U(0,0.25), frequency U(0,3) Hz, random phase) to recorded rest/postural tremor
participants_or_bench: 81 PD and ET patients, 250 assessments, 87.5 h; Noraxon 3-axis accelerometer on the dorsum of the hand at 1500 Hz, down-sampled to 100 Hz
key_quantitative_findings: MSE (test) 0.00104 per segment; 0.00049 for the last sample (forward cells, online use); validation 0.00111. Normalised-MSE improvement vs BMFLC / E-BMFLC / WAKE: +89.58% / +89.01% / +91.07% (test), +88.42% / +87.78% / +90.18% (validation), p=5.96E-08. Horizon one sample = 10 ms. Output power above 3 Hz strongly reduced. Inference latency, parameter count and hardware not reported; authors note it needs 'relatively stronger computational support' (cloud approach proposed).
units_and_conditions: Accelerometer-derived hand motion in normalised units; MSE on synthesised voluntary component; offline
locator: Methods (dataset, data preparation, architecture); Table 2 (MSE); Table 3 (improvements); Discussion (compute)
limitations: Semi-synthetic ground truth (voluntary = random sinusoids <=3 Hz); one-step horizon; offline; backward (bidirectional) cells unusable online; compute unreported; Ibrahim et al. 2021 state it needs 100-150 ms before it estimates properly (secondary claim)
relevance_to_design: Largest pathological-tremor dataset; shows learned models beat Fourier-type estimators on this benchmark
transferability_reason: Voluntary motion modelled as <=3 Hz sinusoids does not represent handwriting strokes; 10 ms horizon is shorter than realistic pen latency; likely too large for a pen MCU; no hardware loop
design_implication: Do not adopt without re-benchmarking on causal pen/handwriting data at the measured delay; useful as an offline teacher or for dataset characterisation
search_query: WebSearch: Shahtalebi PHTNet "Characterization and Deep Mining of Involuntary Pathological Hand Tremor using Recurrent Neural Network Models" Scientific Reports 2020

topic: Causal tremor estimation: WAKE wavelet + adaptive Kalman one-step predictor
citation: Shahtalebi S, Atashzar SF, Patel RV, Mohammadi A. WAKE: Wavelet decomposition coupled with adaptive Kalman filtering for pathological tremor extraction. Biomed Signal Process Control. 2019;48:179-188.
task_or_setup: Real-time tremor prediction scheme (wavelet decomposition of the last 2^J samples, J=5, plus adaptive Kalman/AR model, Yule-Walker order p=17) predicts one sample ahead; hyper-parameter adaptation on 5 s windows; offline evaluation on synthetic data (10 signals, 100 Hz, tremor 6-14 Hz), Motus gyroscope data and a smartphone-accelerometer PD dataset
participants_or_bench: Motus dataset 5 subjects with tremor (100 Hz gyroscope); smartphone dataset 10 PD patients; synthetic signals
key_quantitative_findings: Motus dataset NRMSE (mean of 5): BMFLC 0.1046, E-BMFLC 0.0741, WAKE 0.0437; window L=5 s chosen (minimum NRMSE 0.0378 at L=9 s); horizon one sample (10 ms at 100 Hz); no latency or compute figures.
units_and_conditions: NRMSE of tremor estimate; gyroscope angular velocity at 100 Hz; offline
locator: Abstract; Sec 3.2 (RTP scheme); Sec 4.1 and Figs 2-3 (parameters); Sec 4.2.2 Table 2
limitations: One-step horizon; offline; small real datasets; no in-loop test
relevance_to_design: Causal adaptive estimator with reported gain over (E-)BMFLC at modest compute
transferability_reason: Causal and plausibly MCU-feasible, but only 10 ms ahead and never tested in a control loop or on writing
design_implication: Include as a mid-complexity candidate; extend to multi-step prediction equal to measured pen latency before comparing

topic: Learned multi-step voluntary-motion prediction vs WFLC in a closed-loop bench (Parkinsonian tremor)
citation: Ibrahim A, Zhou Y, Jenkins ME, Trejos AL, Naish MD. Real-time voluntary motion prediction and Parkinson's tremor reduction using deep neural networks. IEEE Trans Neural Syst Rehabil Eng. 2021;29:1413-1423.
task_or_setup: 1D-CNN-MLP (2 CNN layers x 64 filters + 1 MLP layer) on IMU angular velocity predicts voluntary motion 10-100 steps ahead; bench: two coupled Maxon EC-max 16 motors (29:1), one replays recorded PD finger motion, the other is commanded by the model or by WFLC; model set to predict 50 ms ahead to cover data-processing and motor delay
participants_or_bench: 18 PD participants (12 train, 3 validation, 3 test); IMUs on hand/wrist at 100 Hz; tasks include resting, pencil pinching/moving and spiral drawing; bench replay of all 18
key_quantitative_findings: Estimation accuracy (EPA) 99.2% (RMSE 0.000313 deg/s). Prediction accuracy (PPA) 97.0 / 94.0 / 91.7 / 90.6% at 10 / 20 / 50 / 100 steps = 100 / 200 / 500 / 1000 ms (abstract gives 91.6 / 89.9% for 50 / 100 steps); prediction time as low as 1.5 ms for 100 steps (desktop PC; i7-9700 CPU, RTX 2060 used for training). Bench tremor PSD reduction 93.8+/-1.5% (model) vs 68.8+/-7.5% (WFLC); voluntary-tracking RMSE 0.07 vs 3.7 deg/s; RMSE rose from 0.012 (simulation) to 0.12 deg/s (bench).
units_and_conditions: Joint angular velocity (deg/s); ground-truth voluntary motion = 2 Hz low-pass applied zero-phase offline, tremor = 3-17 Hz band; PPA = (1-|true-pred|/|true|)x100; motor-pair bench, not a hand or pen
locator: Abstract; Sec I (delay and prior-work claims); Sec III.A-C (data, preparation, metrics); Sec IV (Tables I-III); Sec V.A-C (Figs 8-17, 50 ms horizon, 1.5 ms prediction time)
limitations: Voluntary motion defined as <=2 Hz; PPA metric dominated by slow component; rotary bench without contact; model size not stated; inference timed on a desktop PC
relevance_to_design: Only learned predictor here compared in-loop with WFLC under an explicit ~50 ms delay budget
transferability_reason: Multi-step prediction to cover measured latency is exactly what a pen needs, but the <=2 Hz voluntary definition conflicts with handwriting content, signals are joint angular velocities not nib displacement, and compute is desktop-class
design_implication: Plan predictors with horizon >= measured loop delay; redefine ground truth for handwriting (voluntary strokes may overlap the tremor band); benchmark MCU-class inference latency and memory

topic: Learned tremor prediction: LSTM phase/amplitude forecasting in essential tremor
citation: Pascual-Valdunciel A, Lopo-Martinez V, Sendra-Arranz R, et al. Prediction of pathological tremor signals using long short-term memory neural networks. IEEE J Biomed Health Inform. 2022.
task_or_setup: 180 LSTM models (neurons, layers, input length, prediction horizon, learning rate) trained to predict wrist flexion-extension tremor for timing closed-loop peripheral electrical stimulation
participants_or_bench: 12 ET patients (kinematic data)
key_quantitative_findings: Correlation between predicted and actual tremor 0.709-0.998; phase delay between predicted and real signals <15 ms (~7.5% of a tremor cycle); prediction horizon had the largest effect on performance; 32-56% lower phase-prediction error than the out-of-phase method. Sampling rate and horizon values not stated in abstract.
units_and_conditions: Wrist joint kinematics; offline
locator: Abstract (Europe PMC PMID 36170410)
limitations: Abstract only (open copies behind bot challenge / IEEE 418); application is stimulation timing, not displacement cancellation
relevance_to_design: Evidence that LSTM can forecast ET tremor phase with <15 ms phase error
transferability_reason: Phase/amplitude forecasting of ET tremor is what a nib canceller needs, but wrist kinematics, offline evaluation and unknown horizons
design_implication: Include an LSTM in the estimator bake-off and report phase error at pen-relevant horizons (e.g. 10-30 ms) and at the dominant writing-tremor frequencies

topic: Commercial handheld active stabiliser: Liftware (Lift Labs) ACT spoon pilot in essential tremor
citation: Pathak A, Redmond JA, Allen M, Chou KL. A noninvasive handheld assistive device to accommodate essential tremor: a pilot study. Mov Disord. 2014;29(6):838-842.
task_or_setup: Active Cancellation of Tremor (ACT) handle: two DC motors with mechanical yokes move a detachable spoon in horizontal and vertical directions opposite to sensed tremor; tri-axial accelerometer 'embedded in the spoon base'; tasks holding, eating, transferring; device on vs off, randomised order, subject and neurologist blinded; accelerometer logged at 100 Hz, 12 bit
participants_or_bench: 15 ET (9 M, 6 F); accelerometer analysis in 11
key_quantitative_findings: Accelerometer tremor-amplitude reduction 72% (holding), 76% (eating), 71% (transferring); mean 73%. Change in Fahn-Tolosa-Marin TRS (on vs off): holding 1.00+/-0.76 vs 0.27+/-0.70 (P=0.016), eating 1.47+/-1.06 vs 0.13+/-0.64 (P=0.001), transferring 1.33+/-0.82 vs 0.27+/-0.59 (P=0.001); CGI-S improved for eating and transferring, not holding. Device ~100 g, 40x50x175 mm, >90 min battery. Actuator travel, bandwidth and latency not stated. Two subjects with severe tremor (DBS off) could not use the device.
units_and_conditions: Amplitude at the dominant frequency from double-integrated acceleration after 1st-order 2-25 Hz band-pass (measured by the device's own sensor); ET kinetic tremor; free space
locator: Abstract; Methods (ACT prototype, signal processing); Table 2 (change in TRS); Table 3 (accelerometer %)
limitations: Pilot, small n; authors include Lift Labs CEO/inventor, consultant and employee; spoon only; travel not reported; severe tremor excluded by saturation; outcome sensor is on the device
relevance_to_design: Only peer-reviewed human efficacy data for a commercial handheld active stabiliser
transferability_reason: cm-scale travel in free space (see ACT-17) with spill-avoidance goals, versus +/-0.5 mm nib travel in frictional paper contact with trace-accuracy goals
design_implication: Expect severe tremor to saturate +/-0.5 mm travel and define the target population by tremor amplitude at the nib; reuse the blinded on/off design but with trace metrics and independent (not on-device) measurement
search_query: Europe PMC REST: TITLE:"noninvasive handheld assistive device to accommodate essential tremor"

topic: Active vs passive handheld stabilisers head-to-head (essential tremor, eating task)
citation: Adabi K, Ondo W. Evaluation of tremor-assisted eating devices: a comparative study of usability and patient preference in essential tremor. Mov Disord Clin Pract. 2026 (PMID 40665924).
task_or_setup: Ten transfers of pearl couscous from bowl to a cup near the mouth with seven spoons in randomised, unblinded order: S'up (deep bowl), Gyenno (active motorised), weighted 350 g, Tremelo (wearable damper), Steady Spoon, Eli Spoon, control 45 g

Preference rank (1 best): weighted 2.40, S'up 2.55, Gyenno 3.80. Spillage correlated with TETRAS ADL (r=0.69, p<0.001). Authors: 'Simple strategies, including a deeper bowl and heavier spoon, outperformed more complicated counterweight/actuator devices.'

limitations: Unvalidated task; no accelerometry; convenience sample; no blinding; Liftware not tested
relevance_to_design: Head-to-head evidence that an active handheld stabiliser did not beat simple passive design changes
transferability_reason: Eating task and spill outcome; different device class and loads; relevant mainly as a benchmark-design lesson
design_implication: Benchmark the pen against the best passive pens (weighted, thick, damped) and pre-register a minimum clinically meaningful margin on trace metrics

topic: Active anti-tremor pen: pendulum pen-rod actuated inside casing (control design)
citation: Ou C, Gouldstone A, Jaeger BK, Sipahi R. Control design for a hand tremor suppression pen. Proc ASME Dynamic Systems and Control Conference (DSCC2015), Columbus OH, 2015; paper DSCC2015-9962.
task_or_setup: Model of a pendulum-like pen-rod swinging inside a tubular casing with compliance and active actuation between rod and casing; 2-DOF dynamics (casing translates under tremor-induced force; rod translates and rotates); arbitrary pole placement impossible, so gains found by nonlinear optimisation
participants_or_bench: None (simulation); no hardware results found
key_quantitative_findings: Pen-tip deviation minimised to about -47 dB under tremor-induced cyclic disturbance; settling time about 1 s after impulsive perturbation; controller effort about 2 N. Travel, bandwidth, sensing and paper contact not stated in abstract.
units_and_conditions: dB reduction of pen-tip deviation (reference and tremor model not given in abstract); actuator force in N
locator: Abstract (full text not accessible: ASME Digital Collection and ResearchGate returned HTTP 403)
limitations: Simulation only; contact friction, sensor delay and noise apparently not modelled (not in abstract); single publication
relevance_to_design: Only located control-design study for a pen with an actively actuated tip relative to the casing; gives an order-of-magnitude actuator effort
transferability_reason: Same architecture class as our pen, but an idealised model whose -47 dB is unlikely to survive friction, delay and saturation

topic: Active anti-tremor pen: in-pen linear voice-coil actuator moving the pen point (bench rig on paper)
citation: Yusop ZM, Md Zain MZ, Hussein M, Musa AR, Ishak I. Assistive pen to improve quality writing of hand tremor with proportional-control. Int J Mater Mech Manuf. 2015;3(1):56-59.
task_or_setup: Pen with a linear voice-coil actuator (LVCA) in its rear moving the pen point left-right through joints/bearings; MMA7361 accelerometer inside the pen; proportional control on 0.175-15 Hz 2nd-order Butterworth band-passed acceleration via NI PCI-6259 and LabVIEW; pen mounted on a rig whose separate LVCA (h2w NCC05-11-011-1X, 14.7 N peak, +/-3 V) replays recorded tremor while a DC-motor lead screw draws a straight line on paper
participants_or_bench: Bench; tremor signal recorded from 1 PD participant (38-year-old male) writing with an accelerometer-instrumented pen
key_quantitative_findings: Acceleration PSD peak at 8.667 Hz reduced by 56.57% (Kp 0.42), 55.46% (0.40), 52.48% (0.38), 44.04% (0.35). Straight-line trace: uncontrolled deviation averaged 4.2 mm; with Kp 0.42 'the average of reduction is 2mm, roughly'. In-pen actuator travel/force, loop rate, latency and nib normal load not stated; LVCA magnetic field disturbed the in-pen accelerometer.
units_and_conditions: Pen-body acceleration PSD (single axis); ink-trace deviation on paper in mm (averaging method not stated); tremor ~8.7 Hz
locator: Sec II (rig, LVCAs, accelerometer, participant); Sec III (filter, P control); Sec IV Fig. 4 (PSD %); Sec V Fig. 5 (traces)
limitations: Single recording, single axis, rig not handheld, P-control only, loosely defined metrics, no statistics
relevance_to_design: Only located physical prototype that actuates the writing point with a voice coil and reports an ink-trace effect on paper
transferability_reason: Closest physical analogue (in-pen voice coil, paper contact, tremor replay) but 1-axis rig, unknown normal load and weak metrology
design_implication: Replicate this bench concept properly: 2 axes, controlled 0.2-2 N normal load, calibrated trace metrology, closed-loop nib position sensing; magnetically shield or relocate the IMU away from voice coils

topic: Smart pen for PD handwriting tremor: adaptive filtering with vibration motor (no nib actuation)
citation: Tironi JC, Fernandes A, Borges RC, Silva LA, Parreira WD. A smart pen prototype with adaptive algorithms for stabilizing handwriting tremor signals in Parkinson's disease. Sci Rep. 2025.
task_or_setup: Pen body with ADXL345 accelerometer, Teensy 4.1 MCU and a 3 V coin vibration motor (up to 9000 rpm) described as providing 'haptic feedback'; Fx-LMS, Fx-NLMS, Fx-NLMS&LMS, RLS and Kalman filters simulated on NewHandPD handwriting signals; Kalman implemented on the MCU and tested on an orbital shaking table (constant and variable speed)
participants_or_bench: Signals of 31 PD patients from NewHandPD (200 Hz); no human testing of the prototype
key_quantitative_findings: Simulation: RLS lowest MSE about -53 dB; Kalman converged about 8x faster (about 50 vs 300 iterations). MCU: steady-state MSE about -37 dB (constant tremor) and -26 dB (variable). The nib is not moved; no measurement of physical vibration reduction, ink trace or latency.
units_and_conditions: MSE (dB) of the adaptive filter's digital error signal; desired signal not explicitly defined; shaking-table amplitude/frequency not reported
locator: Methods; Table 1; Figs 5-6; Limitations ('have not involved human participants')
limitations: No humans, no ink/trace or mechanical outcome; role of motor (cue vs counter-vibration) unclear
relevance_to_design: Shows MCU-class real-time Kalman/RLS tremor tracking in a pen body; it is not mechanical stabilisation
transferability_reason: Digital signal smoothing plus haptic cue; provides no evidence about moving a nib against paper
design_implication: Cite only as evidence that Kalman/RLS tracking fits a Teensy-class MCU; never as evidence that a pen can stabilise ink

topic: Passive inertial/spring-isolated tremor pen: observed nib-paper contact behaviour
citation: Dessau PM. Writing pen for essential tremors patients. MS thesis, Mechanical Engineering, California State University, Sacramento; 2012 (committee chair A. Kumagai).
task_or_setup: Passive pen: weighted inner pen holder suspended by rubber-band springs inside an outer shell (shell ID 35 mm, OD 42.5 mm, length 147.5 mm; ~0.226 kg found best by trial); informal tests drawing horizontal, vertical and spiral lines vs regular, ergonomic and weighted pens, an earlier tremor pen and a drafting arm
participants_or_bench: 15 people with tremor tested with members of International Essential Tremor Foundation groups in Roseville CA and Phoenix AZ (diagnosis breakdown ambiguous in text: 'but one of the persons had Essential Tremors (ET). One had neither Parkinson's nor ET'), plus designer testing
comparator: Regular, ergonomic, weighted pens; drafting arm
key_quantitative_findings: No quantitative tremor reduction reported. Observations: 'The pen tip does not vibrate on the paper when the shell is vibrating when the inner assembly is weighted with 8 oz. or 0.2268 kg'; 'the inertia of the weight assembly combined with the static and dynamic friction of a standard ball point pen tip on the paper are the components that prevent the pen from shaking'; because the pen tip constrains the inner assembly it acts as a pivot and vibration was transferred to the top springs, adding vibration at the tip until top stiffness was increased; 'The pen tip encounters to [sic] most static friction during these maneuvers [curves] and tends to release, uncontrollably while negotiating the curve'; lighter pen pressure on small curves helped; ergonomic and weighted pens gave the most positive results; outcomes 'highly variable' and a learning curve was needed.
units_and_conditions: Qualitative user feedback forms; ballpoint on paper
locator: Abstract pp. iv-v; p. 6 (tip does not vibrate on paper with 8 oz inner assembly); p. 10 (shell dimensions); p. 12 (8 oz best; inertia plus nib-paper friction statement); p. 15 (tip acts as pivot); p. 16 (static friction, uncontrolled release on curves, learning curve); pp. 19-20 (participants, ergonomic/weighted pens best, lighter pressure)
limitations: Passive device; informal, unblinded, no quantitative metrics
relevance_to_design: Only located source describing a decoupled nib meeting paper: friction grounds the nib, the tip acts as a pivot, and stick-slip release occurs on curves
transferability_reason: Same ballpoint-on-paper contact physics as our pen, so the qualitative failure modes should transfer, although the evidence is weak and the device is passive
design_implication: Model and test stick-slip explicitly: a compliant or actively 'soft' nib will stick then release on curves; regulate or sense normal load, and treat nib-paper friction as a potential ally (passive grounding) as well as a disturbance

topic: VCM - miniature moving-coil linear actuator (brief-specified part)
citation: Moticont. LVCM-010-013-01 Linear Voice Coil Motor: product page and metric drawing LVCM-010-013-01M (revision field blank; undated).
task_or_setup: Manufacturer specification table and continuous-force-vs-stroke curve for a 9.5 mm OD housed moving-coil VCM
participants_or_bench: not applicable (manufacturer data; test method not published)
comparator: Other sub-15 mm VCMs (AMF-02 to AMF-05)
key_quantitative_findings: Continuous force 0.28 N; intermittent force 0.88 N at 10% duty; force constant Kf 0.29 N/A; back-EMF 0.29 V/(m/s); stroke 6.4 mm; coil clearance 0.33 mm per side; coil resistance 1.9 ohm; inductance 0.2 mH at 1 kHz; max continuous power 1.8 W; coil assembly 2.5 g; body 3.8 g; housing OD 9.5 mm x 12.7 mm, 20.7 mm overall at mid-stroke. Continuous force falls to about 0.18 N at the stroke end (read from plot). MY CALCULATION: Km = Kf/sqrt(R) = 0.29/sqrt(1.9) = 0.21 N/sqrt(W) (check: 0.28 N/sqrt(1.8 W) = 0.21); holding 0.3 N needs about 2.0 W (1.03 A); 1.6 N needs about 58 W (5.5 A, 10.5 V).
units_and_conditions: All values at 25 degC (drawing note); continuous rating presumably free air; max coil temperature and thermal resistance not published
locator: Drawing LVCM-010-013-01M: specification table (lower left) and continuous-force plot
limitations: Thermal resistance, max coil temperature and test method not published; no revision letter; force varies with stroke position.
relevance_to_design: Fits a 10-13 mm bore, but shows that direct-drive VCM force at this size is far below the 0.3-1.6 N transverse load at acceptable power.
transferability_reason: Same size class, voltage and load regime as the pen actuator; per-unit manufacturer data.
design_implication: Reject as nib actuator: even a lever giving nib Km 2.26 N/sqrt(W) (0.5 W at 1.6 N) would need a ratio of about 11:1, which is more than its +/-3.2 mm stroke allows for +/-0.5 mm at the nib (my calc).

topic: Actuator figure of merit and flexure safety factor (moving-magnet actuator + flexure)
citation: Hiemstra DB, Parmar G, Awtar S. Performance Tradeoffs Posed by Moving Magnet Actuators in Flexure-Based Nanopositioning. IEEE/ASME Transactions on Mechatronics (accepted-manuscript PDF).
task_or_setup: Lumped magnetostatic derivation of moving-magnet-actuator tradeoffs, then design, build and test of a single-axis flexure nanopositioner
participants_or_bench: Bench prototype: MMA plus double-parallelogram flexure bearing
comparator: Piezo stacks, quasi-static and ultrasonic piezomotors, voice-coil actuators (literature review in paper)
key_quantitative_findings: Actuator constant (force per sqrt(power)) is the traditional figure of merit. For traditional MMAs, force is proportional to sqrt(moving-magnet mass) x sqrt(power), which defines a 'dynamic actuator constant'. Flexure beams 0.75 x 25.4 x 80 mm give motion stiffness 3.43 N/mm and +/-5 mm stroke with a safety factor of 4 against yielding (natural frequency 25 Hz). The system achieved 10 mm range, 4 nm resolution and less than 0.5 degC temperature rise with a passive thermal-management system. Ultrasonic piezomotors reach 100-500 mm/s but under 10 N, and quasi-static and ultrasonic piezomotors have low fatigue life (cited).
units_and_conditions: As reported; macro-scale stage
locator: Abstract; Sec. II-A (actuator review); Sec. III (tradeoffs); flexure design and thermal-management sections (pp. 1-3, 8)
limitations: Macro-scale nanopositioner rather than pen scale; piezomotor statements are literature citations.
relevance_to_design: Supports ranking actuators by Km and moving mass, treating thermal management as first-order, and a flexure safety factor of about 4 on yield.
transferability_reason: The scaling laws transfer; geometry and thermal environment differ.
design_implication: Rank candidates by nib-referred Km and reflected moving mass; design flexures with safety factor 4 or more on yield (static), then check fatigue separately (see AMF-19, AMF-26).

participants_or_bench: not applicable
comparator: Fixed-supply linear VCM drivers (prior art described)
key_quantitative_findings: The OIS actuator stroke command is 'up to 200 microns'. The VCM driver 'may be any suitable linear or switch mode current driver'. The VCM driver of a smartphone 'spends the majority of its time ... driving less than 50% of its maximum output current', and driver heat at low output current is a thermal problem (the motivation for a variable supply voltage). Coil resistance and force values: not published.
units_and_conditions: Descriptive; no test conditions
locator: Detailed description (Google Patents full text)
limitations: No coil resistance, force or current values; a patent is not bench data.
relevance_to_design: Places OIS VCMs at about 0.2 mm stroke with light loads, and shows that linear current drivers waste heat.

topic: Flexure design guidance - allowable deflection vs yield and safety factor
citation: Awtar S. Synthesis and Analysis of Parallel Kinematic XY Flexure Mechanisms. PhD thesis, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, February 2004.
task_or_setup: Beam-flexure design limits and material selection for an XY flexure stage
participants_or_bench: Analytical; AL6061-T651 prototype discussed
key_quantitative_findings: With the maximum-shear-stress yield criterion, max allowable tip displacement is Delta/L <= (1/(3*eta)) * (Sy/E) * (L/T), where eta is a safety factor chosen for stress concentration. L/T ratios of 50 are common. Sy/E ranges from 4e-3 (AL-6061) to 1e-2 (Ti). Typical max deformation is 0.05L-0.1L, but in practice it is kept well within this when fatigue loading is considered. Beryllium copper has an excellent Sy/E but was rejected for fabricability; AL6061-T651 was chosen for low internal stress.
units_and_conditions: Static yield criterion; fatigue treated qualitatively
locator: Sec. 3, eq. (3.2) (PDF p. 56); material selection (PDF p. 158)
limitations: Static yield basis; no numeric fatigue allowable; Smith (2000) and Howell (2001) texts were not accessed.
relevance_to_design: Gives the sizing relation linking flexure length and thickness to the +/-0.5 mm stroke at a chosen stress.
transferability_reason: Beam mechanics are scale-independent.
design_implication: Size flexure beams on the fatigue allowable (about 150 MPa for C17200 TH04) in place of Sy/eta. MY CALC example: a fixed-guided beam has sigma = 3*E*T*delta/L^2, so L >= sqrt(3*T*delta/alpha) with alpha = sigma/E = 150/127600 = 1.18e-3. For T = 0.1 mm and delta = 0.5 mm, L >= 11.3 mm; for T = 0.05 mm, L >= 8.0 mm.

topic: normal force (axial) - healthy adults
citation: Schomaker LRB, Plamondon R. The relation between pen force and pen-point kinematics in handwriting. Biological Cybernetics 63:277-289
task_or_setup: Cursive Dutch word 'gestaakt' (10 reps) plus drawing patterns (finger lines, wrist lines, CW/CCW circles 5-6 mm, scribbles), 12 s trials at normal pace; lab stylus with strain-gauge axial force transducer (0-10 N) holding a normal ballpoint refill, writing on A4 paper placed on a Calcomp 9000 tablet (105.2 Hz); forearm fixed in a cuff

comparator: Between patterns (cursive vs simple drawing) and between subjects
key_quantitative_findings: Axial pen force (APF) while writing the cursive word: per-subject means 57-212 g (0.56-2.08 N); mean of the 16 subject means 103 g = 1.01 N, between-subject SD 44 g = 0.43 N, median 96 g = 0.94 N (computed by CON from Table 4a); within-word SD 11-25 g (0.11-0.25 N), mean 18 g. Condition means (Table 2): scribbles 83.6 g, wrist lines 87.5 g, CW circles 108.9 g, cursive 109.7 g (variance 806 g^2, highest), finger lines 113.5 g, CCW circles 115.3 g. Within a trial (maximum 12 s; mean word duration 4.9 s) APF drifted +8 g/s in cursive (linear-fit start 91.6 g, end 127.7 g) and -1 to -2 g/s in drawing patterns. APF only weakly coupled to kinematics (coherence <0.5; mean r(APF, finger displacement) = -0.23).
units_and_conditions: grams-force along the pen axis (APF), not normal to the page (1 g = 9.81 mN); transducer low-pass 2nd-order Butterworth -3 dB at 17.5 Hz, 10-bit; paper on digitiser (hard underlay); forearm immobilised
locator: Methods 2.1-2.2; Results; Table 2 (preprint p.30) and Table 4a (p.31)

relevance_to_design: Direct measure of the axial contact load the moving nib must carry during natural cursive writing with a ballpoint on paper
transferability_reason: Ballpoint refill on paper, adult writers, force measured at the refill exactly where our actuator sits; only posture restriction and underlay differ
design_implication: Use ~1.0 N nominal axial load, between-writer 0.5-2.1 N, within-word SD ~0.2 N and slow upward drift within words when sizing the nib support, actuator holding force and any force sensing

topic: pen tilt angle; friction; force/kinematic spectra
citation: Schomaker LRB, Plamondon R. The relation between pen force and pen-point kinematics in handwriting. Biological Cybernetics 63:277-289 (angle, friction and spectral results)
task_or_setup: As CON-01; additional control recordings with a modified tablet controller giving pen angle (accuracy 3 deg), T = 9 s
participants_or_bench: 16 students (spectra); 4 subjects (pen-angle control test)
comparator: Axial vs normal pen force; kinematic vs force spectra

Friction: cites Dooijes (1984) estimate that ballpoint friction is about 4% of normal pen force in the 0-2 N range. Spectra: all kinematic and dAPF power spectra peak at 2-5 Hz; scribbling peak 4.5 Hz, circling 3.5 Hz; dAPF has relatively more power above 8 Hz (attributed to friction hysteresis and paper irregularities). Authors quote 8-12 strokes/s for adult cursive.
units_and_conditions: Angle between pen long axis and writing plane (altitude); F_N = F_A x sin(angle); spectra of differentiated signals, resolution 0.103 Hz (patterns) / 0.411 Hz (words)
locator: Introduction pp.3-4; Results p.16 (pen-angle control); Results pp.14-15 (PSDFs); Discussion pp.21-22 (Dooijes friction estimate; strokes/s)
limitations: Angle result from only 4 subjects with fixed forearm; the 4% friction figure is a secondary citation of Dooijes (1984), not re-measured; strokes/s is a statement, not tabulated
relevance_to_design: Gives pen altitude for converting axial to normal/lateral load, shows tilt is nearly constant within writing, and flags that contact-force signals carry >8 Hz texture/friction content

P3040 tracks up to 200 mm from the surface but 'increasingly unreliably above a distance of 60 mm'; trackable surface typically detected within 20 mm; clutch by lifting ~2 cm. Tip PCB 10 mm x 12 mm; pen 190 mm long, 15 mm diameter. Both sensors on one 3-wire SPI bus. Accelerometer logged at 200 Hz, magnetometer at 100 Hz; FSR sampled at 200 Hz (13-bit ADC). Raw-flow outliers ~0.05% of samples (rejected by thresholding). Rotation: d_alpha = arcsin( s x (s+o) / (|s|*|s+o|) ), s = vector between optical centres, o = difference of the two sensors' motion vectors; tilt ('DPI') correction dx = x_raw/cos(theta), dy = y_raw/cos(psi) from the gravity vector; tip-offset compensation. End-to-end latency stated only as 'comparable to the latency of a tethered computer mouse' (no number). Sensor baseline |s| NOT reported numerically (bounded by the 10 x 12 mm PCB; diagonal 15.6 mm, derived). No numeric tilt limits reported.

topic: Pen-tip optical flow: Flashpen (PMW3360 in a pen tip)
citation: Romat H., Fender A., Meier M., Holz C. (2021). Flashpen: A High-Fidelity and High-Precision Multi-Surface Pen for Virtual Reality. IEEE VR 2021, pp. 306-315.
task_or_setup: Pen with a PixArt PMW3360 gaming-mouse sensor at the tip (lens and cover sanded down; flat tip on a cut LEGO hinge with 110 deg range), MPU6500 IMU and ESP32 tethered to a PC; flow sensor used on-surface, 2 OptiTrack Flex13 cameras give hover position and absolute yaw; tracing and writing blocks vs a Wacom pen.
participants_or_bench: 10 participants (4 female), aged 23-36 (mean 29.6)
comparator: Wacom professional drawing tablet pen; ordinary pen on paper (writing block)
key_quantitative_findings: Sensor run at 8,000 fps in burst mode; NOMINAL motion resolution stated as 1/226 mm (4.42 um); authors compare with ~200 Hz tablet digitisers. MEASURED tracing accuracy (mean shortest distance to reference normalised by shape width of 1/2/3 cm): ACCURATE instruction Flashpen 0.028 vs Wacom 0.026; FAST instruction 0.076 vs 0.079; no device x speed interaction (F1,9 = 0.80, p = 0.393). Pen mass ~200 g. Authors: works on 'most surface types (wood, paper, plastic and many more)', not glass.
units_and_conditions: Absolute yaw from cameras throughout (flow alone cannot give page orientation); tethered; Oculus Quest 2 via Link.
locator: Abstract; Sec. 3.1-3.2 (pp.3-4), Fig. 2-3; Sec. 5.1 (Block 1 results); Sec. 7 Limitations
limitations: Flat mouse-like contact tip, not a ballpoint; relies on external cameras for yaw and hover; writing block weaker than tracing; surface list qualitative; heavy prototype.
relevance_to_design: Shows a lens-based gaming sensor reaches tablet-like tracing fidelity at 8 kHz - but only with a flat contact tip at fixed height and an external yaw reference.
transferability_reason: Same sensor class; tip geometry and dependence on external tracking differ from a stand-alone ballpoint stabiliser.
design_implication: Use PMW33xx-class sensors on the bench rig (fixed Z) as the high-rate reference; in a ballpoint pen they need custom optics or a lens-less part; provide yaw from a second flow sensor or IMU/magnetometer rather than assuming it.

PMW3389: up to 16,000 cpi (50 cpi steps), 400 ips typ, 50 g, Z 2.2-2.6 mm, lift cut-off 2 or 3 mm, run current 21 mA incl. LED at VDD 1.9 V, package 10.90 x 16.20 x 5.01 mm, self-adjusting frame rate (maximum not in key parameters). Both datasheets plot mean resolution and path error versus Z (about 2.0-2.9 mm), i.e. the count scale depends on height.

design_implication: Put a PMW3360/3389 on a fixed-height carriage in the bench rig (8-12 kHz frames, ~0.1 ms read latency); do not base the product on them unless custom optics hold Z within +/-0.2 mm across tilt.

topic: Capture pens: Anoto dot-pattern principle (patents and open codec)
citation: Anoto AB patents US6548768B1 'Determination of a position code' (priority 1999-10-01; published 2003-04-15) and US6663008B1 'Coding pattern and apparatus and method for determining a value of at least one mark of a coding pattern' (priority 1999-10-01; granted 2003-12-16); Heindl C., py-microdots (MIT-licensed Anoto codec) README.
task_or_setup: Absolute position coding: one mark per nominal raster point, displaced in one of four directions; the pen camera images a small window and decodes absolute x,y.
participants_or_bench: Patent embodiments; open-source reimplementation
key_quantitative_findings: Raster spacing 300 um (range 250-300 um; 254 um variant for printers at multiples of 100 dpi); mark displacement 50 um (1/6 of the raster); embodiment sensor 'provides a new image every tenth millisecond' (~100 images/s) and sees about 10-12 marks per direction; example coding window of 4x4 symbols = 4^16 = 4,294,967,296 positions. py-microdots (describing the deployed pattern): every 6x6 dot window encodes a unique position at 0.3 mm grid (1.8 mm x 1.8 mm window, derived), unique over an area comparable to Europe and Asia. Positioning accuracy of commercial pens: NOT stated in these sources. Rough derivation: resolving 50 um offsets needs object-space sampling of roughly 25 um/pixel or finer.
units_and_conditions: Patent embodiments, not product specifications.
locator: US6548768B1 description (raster, displacement, image rate); US6663008B1 definitions and coding example; py-microdots README
limitations: Embodiments may differ from the commercial pattern; 6x6 details come from a third-party codec; no measured accuracy; the Google Patents record for US6548768B1 shows an expiry date of 2021-08-22, but freedom-to-operate for later Anoto patents was not assessed.
relevance_to_design: Printed-pattern paper gives the absolute page coordinates that note capture needs and relative flow cannot provide.
transferability_reason: Decoding physics transfers; using Anoto's pattern space is contractual; a self-made pattern needs its own IP review.
design_implication: Treat a printed position pattern as the proven route to absolute capture; if a tip camera is designed, target <= ~25 um/pixel object sampling and >= 75 Hz; commission a freedom-to-operate review before any own-pattern design.

topic: Inertial pens: why absolute position is unobservable (error-growth derivation)
citation: Analytical derivation in this ledger using STMicroelectronics LSM6DSL datasheet DocID028475 Rev 6 (May 2017) - the accelerometer/gyroscope in the STABILO DigiPen (see OPT-15).
task_or_setup: Dead-reckoning position error from double integration of accelerometer output, using datasheet offset and noise figures.
participants_or_bench: n/a (calculation)
comparator: Optical-flow drift: DeltaPen idle translation drift 0.04375 mm/s (OPT-02)
key_quantitative_findings: Datasheet: zero-g offset +/-40 mg typ; zero-rate level +/-3 deg/s; acceleration noise density 90 ug/sqrt(Hz) (+/-2 g, high-performance); rate noise density 4 mdps/sqrt(Hz). Derived: constant accel bias b gives position error b*t^2/2 - 40 mg: 1.96 mm at 0.1 s, 196 mm at 1 s; 1 mg residual: 0.049 mm at 0.1 s, 4.9 mm at 1 s, 490 mm at 10 s. Gyro bias w tilts the gravity reference, error ~ g*w*t^3/6 - 3 deg/s: 0.086 mm at 0.1 s, 85.6 mm at 1 s. White noise alone: sigma_p ~ a_n*t^1.5/sqrt(3) = 0.51 mm at 1 s, 16 mm at 10 s. Accelerometers sense specific force (second derivative of position), so initial position and velocity are unobservable constants; yaw about the paper normal is unobservable from gravity; only short windows or zero-velocity updates (pen still) bound the error. Optical flow senses velocity, so its drift grows ~linearly (DeltaPen 2.6 mm/min idle) rather than quadratically.
units_and_conditions: Order-of-magnitude figures; perfect gravity removal assumed apart from the stated biases; g = 9.80665 m/s^2.
locator: LSM6DSL datasheet Table 3 'Mechanical characteristics' (pp.21-22); derivation in this row
limitations: Calibration, temperature compensation, ZUPT and fusion reduce but do not remove error growth; illustrative, not a measured pen.
relevance_to_design: Explains why inertial sensing can support tremor-band stabilisation (short horizon, high-pass) but cannot deliver page position for note capture.
transferability_reason: Physics independent of implementation.
design_implication: Use the IMU for tilt, tremor-band motion and gaps under ~0.1 s; require optical-flow or pattern sensing for anything longer; exploit pen-still periods for zero-velocity updates.

topic: Grounded generation evaluation: AIS (Attributable to Identified Sources)
citation: Rashkin H., Nikolaev V., Lamm M., Aroyo L., Collins M., Das D., Petrov S., Tomar G.S., Turc I., Reitter D. Measuring Attribution in Natural Language Generation Models. arXiv:2112.12870v2 (2 Aug 2022).
task_or_setup: Defines AIS: output is attributable if a generic reader would agree 'According to P, s'; two-stage human annotation (interpretability, then attribution) on conversational QA, CNN/DM summarisation and table-to-text.
participants_or_bench: Crowd annotators; 200 CNN/DM test examples per system
comparator: Extractive (MatchSum), hybrid (Pointer-Gen), abstractive (BigBird) and reference summaries
key_quantitative_findings: CNN/DM AIS: MatchSum 99.4%, Pointer-Gen 97.8%, BigBird 87.2%, gold reference summaries 54.1% (interpretability 86-90%). Inter-annotator agreement for AIS on CNN/DM: F1 0.92, pairwise agreement 0.89, Krippendorff's alpha 0.69 (interpretability alpha 0.46).
units_and_conditions: Summary-level judgements; percentages of outputs judged attributable.
locator: Sec. 3-4 (definition and pipeline); Table 5 (p.17); Table 7 (p.18)
limitations: News summaries, not personal notes; human-only protocol is costly; arXiv version read.
relevance_to_design: Supplies the definition and protocol for judging whether each summary statement is supported by the user's own notes.
transferability_reason: Source-agnostic definition; the 'source' becomes the note transcript.
design_implication: Adopt AIS-style two-stage human rating (interpretable? attributable to the cited note spans?) as the gold standard and report Krippendorff's alpha.

topic: Grounded generation evaluation: FActScore (atomic-fact precision)
citation: Min S., Krishna K., Lyu X., Lewis M., Yih W., Koh P.W., Iyyer M., Zettlemoyer L., Hajishirzi H. FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation. arXiv:2305.14251v2 (11 Oct 2023).
task_or_setup: Split a generation into atomic facts; score = % of atomic facts supported by a knowledge source; human annotation plus an automated estimator (retrieval + LM).
participants_or_bench: Human annotators on people biographies; automated scoring of 6,500 generations from 13 LMs
key_quantitative_findings: Human FActScore: InstructGPT 42%, ChatGPT 58%, PerplexityAI 71%; automated estimator error rate < 2% vs human FActScore; scoring 6,500 generations with humans would have cost ~USD 26K.
units_and_conditions: Wikipedia as knowledge source; precision only.
locator: Abstract; Sec. 3 (human results); Table 3 (estimator error rates)
limitations: Biographies domain; estimator error higher for rare entities; no recall/coverage measure.
relevance_to_design: Atomic-fact support against the user's notes is a natural faithfulness metric for note summaries.
transferability_reason: Knowledge source becomes noisy recognised text; the estimator must be revalidated on notes.
design_implication: Score atomic facts against both the recognised text and the ground-truth transcript to separate recognition-induced from generation-induced errors.

topic: Grounded generation evaluation: RAGAS (reference-free RAG metrics)
citation: Es S., James J., Espinosa-Anke L., Schockaert S. Ragas: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation. arXiv:2309.15217v2 (28 Apr 2025).
task_or_setup: LLM-based, reference-free metrics: faithfulness (answer statements supported by the retrieved context), answer relevance, context relevance; validated on the WikiEval set against human pairwise judgements.
participants_or_bench: Two human annotators (agreed in ~95% of cases for faithfulness and context relevance, ~90% for answer relevance)
comparator: GPT Score and GPT Ranking baselines
key_quantitative_findings: Agreement with human pairwise judgements (accuracy): faithfulness 0.95, answer relevance 0.78, context relevance 0.70 (GPT Score 0.72 / 0.52 / 0.63; GPT Ranking 0.54 / 0.40 / 0.52).
units_and_conditions: WikiEval; accuracy of pairwise preference.
locator: Sec. 3 (metrics); Sec. 4 (WikiEval); Table 1
limitations: Small evaluation set; depends on the judging LLM; measures faithfulness to retrieved context only.
relevance_to_design: Cheap automated faithfulness check for retrieval-grounded note Q&A and summaries.
transferability_reason: Needs recalibration on noisy handwritten-note text.
design_implication: Use RAGAS-style faithfulness as a regression metric in CI, recalibrated periodically against AIS human labels on our notes.

topic: Grounded generation evaluation: ALCE citation recall/precision and audit of generative search
citation: Gao T., Yen H., Yu J., Chen D. Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations. arXiv:2305.14627v2 (31 Oct 2023) (ALCE); Liu N.F., Zhang T., Liang P. Evaluating Verifiability in Generative Search Engines. arXiv:2304.09848v2 (23 Oct 2023).
task_or_setup: Citation recall (each statement fully supported by its citations, judged by the NLI model TRUE, T5-11B) and citation precision (each citation needed/relevant); human audit of commercial generative search engines.
participants_or_bench: ALCE: human evaluation of model outputs; Liu et al.: human audit of four generative search engines
comparator: Human judgements vs automatic NLI metric
key_quantitative_findings: ALCE: on ELI5 even the best models lack complete citation support ~50% of the time; human-vs-automatic Cohen's kappa 0.698 (citation recall) and 0.525 (citation precision); automatic metric accuracy vs human labels 85.1% (recall) and 77.6% (precision). Liu et al.: 51.5% of generated sentences fully supported by citations; 74.5% of citations support their sentence.
units_and_conditions: Open-domain QA / web search.
locator: ALCE Abstract, Sec. 3 (metrics), Sec. 6 (human evaluation); Liu et al. Abstract
limitations: Not personal notes; NLI models may mishandle misrecognised words.
relevance_to_design: Defines per-statement citation metrics for 'source-grounded' summaries.
transferability_reason: Metric definitions transfer directly; the NLI judge needs validation on noisy notes.
design_implication: Require each summary sentence to cite note/page/stroke spans; report citation recall and precision (NLI plus human audit) and use these published figures as minimum baselines.

participants_or_bench: None (patent disclosure; no test data reported)
key_quantitative_findings: Cl. 1: human tremor compensation system: stabilization unit (base held in the hand with an internal motion-generating mechanism including an actuator; implement portion coupled by an attachment arm and moved relative to the base); at least one remote non-contact position sensor external to and not in contact with the unit, sensing a 3-D position of at least the base; processing unit external to the unit wirelessly transmitting motion commands to move the implement relative to the base to dynamically cancel unintentional muscle movements. units_and_conditions: n/a
locator: Claims 1, 10; description (inertial and hall-effect sensors).
limitations: Claim 1 checked against OCR of the official USPTO image PDF (retrieved 2026-09-27 UTC); claim 2 lists IR/visible/stereo camera, laser displacement or ultrasonic sensor; claim 10 wording not captured. design_implication: Keep sensing and control on-board; attorney to confirm that on-board tip optical sensing is outside 'remote non-contact position sensor external to ... the stabilization unit'.

topic: Handheld micromanipulator (Micron family) with tool-shaft force sensing
citation: Carnegie Mellon University; The Johns Hopkins University (inventors Gonenc B., Iordachita I., Taylor R. H., Riviere C., Gehlbach P., Handa J.). Micromanipulation systems and methods. US 10,369,045 B2, granted 2019-08-06; appl. US 14/810,277 filed 2015-07-27; priority 2014-07-29; also US 2016/0030240 A1. Status: Active, expires 2036-02-08 (as displayed on Google Patents on 2026-09-26; not verified in official register).
task_or_setup: Micron handpiece (piezoelectric tip deflection for tremor cancellation; optical ASAP tracking of the handle) carrying modular motorised tools (forceps, microneedle) with fibre-Bragg-grating force sensors on the tool shaft; processor removes actuation-induced force artefacts to estimate tool-tissue force; auditory force feedback; assistive micro-vibration; puncture detection with position locking.
participants_or_bench: None (patent disclosure; no test data reported)
key_quantitative_findings: Granted claims (OCR of official USPTO PDF): cl. 1 micromanipulation system: handpiece; actuator assembly giving manual control of the tool; tool vibrating system (vibrator assembly + vibration controller); tool with shaft; force sensor on the shaft indicating force on the manipulation end and along the shaft; processor compensating forces due to actuation of the tool to determine the interaction force; vibration controller imposing vibration on the shaft along the direction of that interaction force to facilitate manipulation. Dependent: 2 fibre-optic force sensor; 3 tremor cancellation system with a motor in the handpiece providing active tremor cancellation independently of the vibrations; 4 position detection system reporting micromanipulator position; 5-8 microneedle puncture detection, indication and automatic position holding; 10-15 actuator and tool variants. Cl. 17 method: actuate tool; detect tip and axial forces; determine interaction force compensating actuation forces; indicate magnitude/direction; vibrate the shaft along that direction; 18 simultaneous automatic tremor cancellation; 19 independent electro-mechanical actuation. Description: voluntary 2-4 Hz vs tremor 8-12 Hz; piezo workspace ~1 x 1 x 0.5 mm; FBG interrogated at 1 kHz; micro-vibration 10-50 Hz at 50-150 um.
units_and_conditions: Hz; mm; um
locator: Claims 1-19 (USPTO PDF pp. 69-70 of 70); description.
limitations: Claims read from OCR of the official USPTO image PDF (retrieved 2026-09-27 UTC); the claim 1 first returned by automated extraction omitted the vibration limitation and was discarded. Surgical context. Core Micron tremor-cancellation patents not retrieved (query returned HTTP 503). Status as displayed on Google Patents on 2026-09-26; not verified in official register.
relevance_to_design: Independent claims combine (e) shaft force sensing with actuation-force compensation and vibrating the tool along the sensed force direction; tremor cancellation (a/b-type) and position detection (d-type) appear only in dependent claims 3, 4 and 18; description shows Micron tip-deflection tremor cancellation with external optical tracking.
transferability_reason: Handheld actuated tool with force sensing and tremor cancellation - same physics; microsurgical scale, external tracker, and the claims centre on force-directed vibration.
design_implication: Our design does not vibrate the nib along the sensed force direction, so the independent claims look technically distant (attorney to confirm); keep the record as prior art for actuation-force compensation of a tool force signal. Micron literature is strong general prior art for tip-deflection tremor cancellation.

topic: Position-correcting handheld tool: camera localisation + motorised stage (Shaper)
citation: Shaper Tools, Inc. (inventors Rivers A. R., Moyer I. E.). Automatically guided tools. US 10,078,320 B2, granted 2018-09-18; appl. task_or_setup: Handheld router/tool whose working member sits on a stage moved by motors (two stepper motors with eccentric cams, ~0.5 in correction radius); camera images of the work surface build a map (SLAM, optional marker stickers) and localise the tool; processor drives the stage so the working member follows a design path; printer/marker embodiments described.
participants_or_bench: None (patent disclosure; no test data reported)
key_quantitative_findings: Official claim 1 (OCR of USPTO PDF): system to position a working member of a rig (rig has a stage holding the working member and at least one motor moving the stage): processor with software; one or more sensors, a first sensor capturing first information of a surface of a material; memory; the software determines a first location of the working member using a map of the surface retrieved from memory, indicates that location on a display screen of the rig, registers a design from memory to the map to identify a path, compares the location with the path to determine a second location, controls motor(s) to move the stage so the working member aligns with the path, and controls motor(s) to maintain alignment by moving the working member in a first direction as the rig is advanced in a second, different direction. Dependent (read): 2-3 second sensor capturing images used to build the map (may be the same sensor); 4-5 markers (sticker, ink, invisible ink, projected feature, pencil or marker marking); 6 successive positions while the rig is advanced; 7 rig may be a router, drill, nail gun, jigsaw, scroll saw or printer; working member a cutting bit, saw blade, drill bit, hammer or printer head; first sensor a camera, ultrasonic sensor, IR range finder or laser; 8 image data used to realign toward the preferred next path position; 10-11 display of path and of the working member's range of movement; 15-17 map by stitching images, marker matching. Independent method claim 19 mirrors claim 1. Description: two stepper motors with eccentric cams; correction radius ~0.5 in (~1 in diameter); out-of-range handled by notification and waiting.
units_and_conditions: inch
locator: Claims 1-22 (USPTO PDF pp. 29-30 of 32; claims 1-18 and 19-22 read); description (eccentric-cam stage, SLAM, printer embodiment).
limitations: Claims read from OCR of the official USPTO image PDF (retrieved 2026-09-27 UTC). The claim 1 first returned by automated extraction from Google Patents did NOT match the official grant and was discarded. Continuation claim sets not reviewed. Status as displayed on Google Patents on 2026-09-26; not verified in official register.
relevance_to_design: Claims recite a hand-advanced rig whose motorised stage moves the working member relative to the rig (a-type) to keep it on a design path registered to a stored surface map, using surface-sensing (camera etc.; c-type) and path-following correction while the user advances the tool (g-analogue); range-of-movement display (cl. 11) and out-of-range waiting in the description are analogues of (h).

design_implication: Strong prior art for local correction toward a path while the user advances the tool; attorney to review whether a pen using local optical flow without a stored surface map, without a rig display screen, and with letter templates not registered to a surface map falls outside claims 1/19; review continuation claims (e.g., US 11,815,873 B2) separately.

topic: PD micrographia: prevalence and clinical correlates
citation: Wagle Shukla A, Ounpraseuth S, Okun MS, Gray V, Schwankhaus J, Metzer WS. Micrographia and related deficits in Parkinson's disease: a cross-sectional study. BMJ Open 2012;2(3):e000628.
task_or_setup: Micrographia asked on history, plus a handwriting test: lowercase print 'p' and 'd' written 20 times in two rows (4 blocks of 5); micrographia = area of last block >=30% smaller than first block (severe = >50%). Bradykinesia by finger tap, Purdue pegboard and timed walk; hypophonia by decibel meter. Tested in the usual ON medication state.
participants_or_bench: 68 PD (all men; Veterans Administration movement-disorders clinic; mean age 72.3 +/- 9.5 y; disease duration 7.8 +/- 5.5 y). Excluded: severe tremor, dystonia, dyskinesia, stroke, neuropathy, dementia. Controls used only to validate test scores.
comparator: Self-report vs handwriting test; controls for test validation
key_quantitative_findings: Micrographia on history 63.2% (43/68); on handwriting test ~50% (35/68); severe (>50% area drop) n=12. Test vs history: sensitivity 0.74 (95% CI 0.59-0.86), specificity 0.88 (0.68-0.97). Test-defined micrographia correlated with age (p=0.02), MMSE (p=0.04), hypophonia by history (p=0.01) and quantitative bradykinesia (Purdue pegboard, p=0.04). No correlation with L-DOPA equivalent dose.
units_and_conditions: Area ratio (%) of last vs first block of letters; ON medication; no letter heights in mm reported.
locator: Abstract; Methods (handwriting test, Figure 1); Results (correlates); Discussion (limitations)
limitations: Cross-sectional, single visit; all-male veteran cohort; unblinded raters; ON state only, so medication effect not tested; >=30% area criterion is study-specific; severe-tremor patients excluded.
relevance_to_design: About half of clinic PD patients show a measurable within-task size decrement; the deficit is a size-scaling problem across a sequence of letters, not sub-millimetre positional noise.
transferability_reason: Clinic cohort of older male veterans; prevalence depends on the task and threshold used.
design_implication: A +/-0.5 mm local nib offset cannot restore a 30-50% loss of letter-block area accumulated along a line. Target micrographia with size-feedback and cueing modes. Do not use the pen to detect micrographia.

topic: PD handwriting impairment overview (micrographia, dysgraphia, medication response)
citation: Thomas M, Lenka A, Kumar Pal P. Handwriting Analysis in Parkinson's Disease: Current Status and Future Directions. Mov Disord Clin Pract 2017;4(6):806-818.
task_or_setup: Narrative review of PubMed/SCOPUS literature on kinematic handwriting analysis in PD.
participants_or_bench: n/a (review)
key_quantitative_findings: Definitions: consistent micrographia = 'an overall reduction in letter size compared with that before the onset of PD'; progressive = 'decreasing letter size as writing progresses'. 'The exact prevalence of micrographia in PD is not clear and may range from 9% to 60%'. 'Letter size improves in only 50% of patients in response to medications', whereas velocity, fluency and acceleration measures are more medication-sensitive (Poluha 1998, Tucha 2006, Lange 2006, Table 1). Bajaj et al.: micrographia more prevalent in akinetic-rigid than tremor-dominant PD (90% sensitivity, 55% specificity for the akinetic-rigid phenotype). Rosenblum 2013: PD applied less pen pressure than controls. Fluency measures: NIV/NIA, jerk, ratio of deceleration phase.
units_and_conditions: Percentages (prevalence); qualitative kinematic findings.
locator: Sections 'Spectrum of Handwriting Abnormalities in PD - Micrographia', 'The Concept of PD Dysgraphia', 'Newly Proposed Additional Parameters'; Table 1; Figure 4
limitations: Narrative, non-systematic review; heterogeneous definitions; secondary account of the cited primary studies.
relevance_to_design: PD writing impairment involves size, speed, fluency and pressure. Tremor-dominant PD has less micrographia.
transferability_reason: Review synthesis of heterogeneous tablet studies.
design_implication: Design PD modes around size and fluency, not tremor. Tremor correction matters, if at all, only for the tremor-dominant subgroup. Outcome sets should cover size, velocity, fluency (NIV or jerk) and pressure.
